source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Gillespie_2021_GeneticallyInformedMethods.pdf: online-first version (JAMA Psychiatry, published online 4 November 2020, pp. E1-E2), both pages; pages cited as p. E1 and p. E2. Text extracted with pdftotext -layout (a PDF cross-reference warning did not affect the text); both pages, including the Table and its footnotes, checked on renders at 110 dpi. The print version (2021;78(5):467-468) was not read.

claims.note: Gillespie-sourced figures check against the rendered pages: 10.44 (general population) and 3.52 (discordant monozygotic twins) in the text (p. E1); 10.44, 5.07 (full siblings) and 3.92 (monozygotic twins) in the Table (p. E2); Table footnote e says significance tests were unavailable for monozygotic twin pairs; no adjustment set is given anywhere. The 66% decline given in the text is (10.44 - 3.52)/10.44 = 66.3%, a fall in the OR itself; on the excess-odds scale it is 73% (69% with the Table's 3.92), and with 3.92 the OR decline is 62.5% (second reader's calculations); the claim rightly gives the ORs, not the percentage. Description details not in the viewpoint: it does not say the study was Swedish or registry-based ('Swedish' is in the study's full title as cited by Gage et al., 2016, ref. 26; 'registry-recorded' is in neither source read here), and it calls the exposure 'cannabis misuse' (the cited title says 'cannabis abuse'). Kendler, the viewpoint's second author, is last author of the co-relative study (ref. 4), as the claim says; the viewpoint reports no conflicts of interest. The MR description matches: instruments for lifetime use, not for heavy use or misuse; Vaucher's 37% increase; stronger evidence for the reverse direction in Gage 2017 and Pasman 2018; and the LDSR range 0.22-0.25 includes the claim's 0.25. The viewpoint adds that all three MR studies found no evidence of pleiotropy (Table footnote f), which the claim does not mention. 'Partly causal with an appreciable non-causal share' matches the conclusion. Small wording points: the claim groups this viewpoint with 'narrative reviews' (it is a two-page viewpoint, as the claim says elsewhere); and the co-relative exposure was misuse, the nearest of these designs to heavy use, so 'none measures the effect of frequent ... use' is right only if misuse is not counted as frequent use.

anchors.locator: Natural Experiments, 1st paragraph, end (right column, continuing from the left column) [paragraph count corrected after step 2; passage found in step 1]
anchors.extracted: Only one discordant-relative (co-relative) analysis known to the authors (ref. 4, Giordano et al., 2015, Kendler last author): significantly more schizophrenia with cannabis misuse in the general population, with ORs declining as relatedness increased, from 10.44 in the general population to 3.52 in discordant monozygotic twin pairs, a 66% decline, read as consistent with a partly causal, partly confounded association and as substantial confounding.

anchors.locator: Table, row 'Summary of published results', column 'Discordant sibling pair', and footnote e
anchors.extracted: OR for unrelated pairs 10.44 > full sibling pairs 5.07 > monozygotic twin pairs 3.92 (differs from the 3.52 in the text); tests of significance were unavailable for monozygotic twin pairs; read as consistent with hypothesis 2 (partly causal and confounded).

anchors.locator: Natural Experiments, 2nd paragraph (p. E1, right column); Table, MR column and footnote f (p. E2)
anchors.extracted: Three MR studies: Vaucher et al., genetic liability to lifetime use associated with a 37% higher risk of schizophrenia; Gage et al. (2017) and Pasman et al. (2018), much stronger evidence that genetic liability to schizophrenia increases lifetime use (reverse causation); all rely on variants associated with lifetime use, not heavy use or misuse; all three reported no evidence of pleiotropy; read in aggregate as most consistent with hypothesis 2.

anchors.locator: Measures of genetic association (p. E1, right column, continuing on p. E2, left column); Table, LDSR and PRS columns
anchors.extracted: Two LDSR studies (refs 6, 8) reported significant genetic correlations between lifetime cannabis use or misuse and schizophrenia, range 0.22-0.25; one PRS study in a restricted sample found no effect on cannabis misuse, four large population studies found schizophrenia PRS predicts cannabis and other substance use; modest correlations and small PRS effects, but evidence of confounding inconsistent with an entirely causal association.

Cohorts and meta-analyses show a robust association of cannabis use, heavy use and misuse with later schizophrenia, but covariate-adjusted models can establish causation only as far as they capture all confounders. Conclusion: findings, with considerable but not complete consistency, argue against an entirely causal association and against an entirely non-causal one; the one co-relative study suggests familial confounding accounts for more than half of the association; a prudent reading is some causal effect with an appreciable non-causal share; unadjusted population associations very likely exaggerate risk changes from changing cannabis use; the number of studies is modest.

claims.note: Indirect only: the viewpoint gives no incidence-trend data and is not named in the claim's text. Its one bearing is the call for controlled pre-post designs comparing schizophrenia incidence where cannabis use rose with decriminalization, which implies that such evidence was not yet available; this is consistent with 'evidence is insufficient' and with the claim's point that the existing trend studies are ecological and uncontrolled. If the claim cites this source, the anchor should be 'qualifies'.

anchors.extracted: Further research should include non-genetic approaches, for example controlled pre-post designs examining changes in schizophrenia incidence in states where cannabis use rose after decriminalization, before definitive conclusions are reached.

key_findings.note: Recomputed: OR decline 66.3% (3.52) or 62.5% (3.92); excess odds 73.3% or 69.1%; log OR (ln 10.44 = 2.346) 46.3% or 41.8%, same as the card.
Checked on the rendered p. E2.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in the blind reading.
The Table's MR cell cites 5-7; ref. 7 (Hjorthoj et al., 2019) is the polygenic-score study with no effect described on p. E1; not seen in the blind reading.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high (no search or selection). The 'reliance on own studies' concern is apt: the only co-relative study, which carries the 'more than half' statement, has Kendler as last author, and the viewpoint reports no conflicts.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor, as the conclusion is hedged. The card's point (2) is the strongest: by footnote a's own criterion, telling hypothesis 2 from 3 needs a monozygotic OR significantly above 1, which was not tested (footnote e), yet the Table marks the discordant-pair column 'Hypotheses 2' only; 'good evidence against hypothesis 3' is the most stretched statement in the conclusions.

missed.item: Minor: the card's interpretation-gap summary calls the co-relative study a 'registry study'; the viewpoint does not say so (nor that it was Swedish). The Swedish national design is in the study's full title as cited by Gage et al. (2016), ref. 26.
missed.consequence: If 'Swedish registry' is kept in cl_can_psychosis_causation, it should be anchored to the primary paper (Giordano et al., 2015) or to Gage et al.'s reference, not to this viewpoint.
